inputs.need:
I lead the hospital social work team at a 560-bed general hospital. For older patients with complicated discharges, our social workers sometimes hold a family discharge planning meeting on the ward before the patient goes home: the patient, family members or carers, the nurse in charge, often a therapist and the social worker go through the plan for care at home, equipment, help with medicines and who to call. Whether a meeting happens depends on which social worker has the case, whether the family can come in, and how rushed the discharge is.

Our medical director has asked whether these meetings reduce readmissions within 30 days, because the hospital pays a penalty for early readmissions of patients over 75 and is thinking of making family meetings standard for everyone over 75 with a complicated discharge. My worry is that we tend to hold meetings for the most complicated families, who are also the ones most likely to come back, so a simple comparison could make the meetings look useless or even harmful.

What we have: the hospital's monthly readmission report lists every patient readmitted within 30 days since January 2023, and our social work activity log shows when a family meeting was booked. The log does not say whether the family actually came, who attended or whether a written plan was given; that is only in the social work notes, and reading them takes about fifteen minutes per patient. Two of my senior social workers can give about 120 hours between them to reading notes this winter.

I do not know what kind of study this should be. Can you help me work out a fair way to answer the question with what we have, and what we would need to ask permission for?
inputs.constraints: About 120 hours of senior social worker time for reading notes between November 2026 and February 2027; no contact with patients or families; an answer is needed before the hospital's budget round in May 2027.

response.statement: Hospital social workers hold family discharge planning meetings for some patients aged 75 and over with complicated discharges, and the hospital is considering making them standard to avoid readmission penalties. It is not known locally whether a meeting that the family attends and that ends with a written plan is associated with fewer readmissions within 30 days once the greater complexity of patients chosen for meetings is taken into account. Whether the family attended is recorded only in the social work notes.

Making meetings standard without evidence would take social work time from other patients, while dropping them could remove support that matters to families.
response.currentPractice: Meetings are booked at the discretion of the social worker, more often for complicated families; attendance and plans are written in free-text notes; readmissions are counted monthly without any link to social work activity.
response.whyNow: The medical director wants a recommendation before the budget round in May 2027, and senior social worker time for reading notes is available this winter.
response.constraints: About 120 hours of senior social worker time for reading notes between November 2026 and February 2027; no contact with patients or families; an answer is needed before the hospital's budget round in May 2027.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Older patients go home with a plan their family understands and can carry out, and avoid readmissions that a better plan could prevent.

records.title: Family meetings before hospital discharge and 30-day readmission in adults aged 75 and over: a matched comparison in two hospitals
records.authors: Adebayo-Stroud K, Lindgren-Mwale P, Hartigan-Oyelowo S
records.venue: Journal of Hospital Social Work Practice
records.abstract: We compared 612 patients aged 75 and over who had a documented family discharge meeting with 1,224 patients without a meeting, matched on age, ward and discharge month, in two general hospitals. Thirty-day readmission was 17.8 percent with a meeting and 18.4 percent without. When the analysis was restricted to meetings that a family member attended and that produced a written plan, readmission was 13.1 percent against 18.4 percent. Meetings were more often held for patients with previous admissions and for patients living alone. The authors note that booked meetings and attended meetings are different exposures and that residual confounding by case complexity is likely.

records.title: Confounding by case complexity in evaluations of discharge planning: a methods commentary with a worked example
records.abstract: Patients chosen for enhanced discharge planning usually carry a higher baseline risk of readmission than those who are not, so crude comparisons can make an effective service look harmful. In a worked example from one hospital, the crude odds ratio of 1.35 became 0.82 after adjustment for prior admissions, frailty and living alone. We recommend defining the exposure precisely, measuring the complexity that drives selection before discharge, matching or adjusting on it, and reporting how estimates change as each confounder is added. Unmeasured complexity, such as family conflict, cannot be removed by adjustment and should be discussed openly.

records.title: Structured family involvement in discharge planning for older inpatients: a systematic review of sixteen studies
records.authors: Moreno-Blackwood T, Uchenna-Falk L, Sorensen-Iqbal A
records.abstract: We searched five databases to 2022 for studies of structured family involvement in hospital discharge planning for adults aged 65 and over. Sixteen studies met the inclusion criteria: five randomised trials and eleven observational studies. In the trials, structured family involvement reduced 30-day readmission (pooled risk ratio 0.84, 95 percent CI 0.71 to 0.99). Observational studies were inconsistent, and those that did not adjust for complexity tended to show higher readmission with family involvement. Definitions of family involvement ranged from a single telephone call to a structured meeting with a written plan, and no study reported carers' own outcomes.

records.title: Sampling controls from the discharge population and reading exposure from clinical notes in readmission studies
records.abstract: Readmission studies often need exposure details that exist only in free-text notes. Using a completed study in one hospital, we compared reading notes for every discharge with reading notes only for readmitted patients and a random sample of patients who were not readmitted. Sampling controls at a ratio of two per case reduced note reading by about 80 percent compared with reviewing every discharge, and the odds ratio for the exposure changed by less than 5 percent. Agreement between two readers on whether a family member attended a discharge meeting was good (kappa 0.81). Readers who knew the patient's readmission status coded borderline notes differently.

records.title: Family conferences on medical wards: regional service evaluation summary
records.authors: Regional Health Authority Older People's Services Team
records.venue: Regional Health Authority service evaluation series
records.abstract: This summary describes family conferences held on the medical wards of three hospitals in the region. Conferences brought together the patient, family members, ward staff and a social worker before discharge. Across the three hospitals, 1,140 conferences were held during the evaluation period, and staff surveyed afterwards said conferences improved communication with families. Families were not asked for their views. The summary lists the number of conferences by hospital and month and gives examples of plans agreed. It does not describe how patients were chosen for a conference, what happened after discharge, or when the evaluation period began and ended.

records.title: Carers' experience of discharge planning meetings for older relatives: a qualitative study
records.abstract: We interviewed 28 carers of older relatives discharged from two hospitals about discharge planning meetings. Carers valued meetings that were booked with notice and that ended with a written plan naming who to call. Many working carers could not attend weekday daytime meetings, and carers without a car found the hospital hard to reach; several said they only heard about a meeting after it had happened. Joining by telephone helped some carers but made it harder to ask questions. Carers described being expected to take on care they had not agreed to. The authors conclude that access to meetings is unequal among families.

records.title: Pre-discharge family meetings and early readmission among frail older adults: conference abstract
records.venue: Society for Transitional Care annual meeting abstract book
records.abstract: Background: family meetings before discharge are thought to prevent early readmission. Methods: adults discharged from a teaching hospital were grouped by whether a family meeting was held before discharge. Results: of 140 patients, those with a meeting were readmitted within 30 days less often than those without (12 against 21 percent, p equal to 0.09). Conclusions: family meetings may reduce early readmission and a larger study is planned. The abstract does not state how patients were selected for meetings, the age range, whether the groups were comparable, or whether any adjustment was made, and the listing gives no year of presentation.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, five appraised at abstract level and two left unrated. Trials show a modest reduction in readmission with structured family involvement, while observational comparisons of booked meetings show no difference, probably because meetings are chosen for complex patients; adjustment for complexity reversed a harmful-looking crude estimate in a worked example. Meetings attended by the family and ending with a written plan were followed by lower readmission in one matched comparison. Note reading can identify attendance reliably, and sampling two controls per case keeps reading affordable. Two undated grey records report no usable methods and are not rated.
response.gradeRationale: Trials support a modest benefit of structured family involvement, but local-type evidence on meetings is observational with serious confounding by complexity, and two records could not be rated. Certainty that an attended meeting with a written plan reduces readmission is low.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records; five appraised, two undated records left unrated with no scores; five claims recorded with passages; overall certainty low.

response.reading: Case complexity sits upstream of both the decision to hold a meeting and the risk of readmission, so booked meetings look ineffective or harmful in crude data. The exposure that plausibly protects is a meeting the family attends that ends with a written plan, and it is visible only in notes. Carers' circumstances shape attendance, linking the exposure to deprivation and work. Trials support a modest benefit, the local question is whether it holds in routine practice.

response.finer: Feasible with 120 hours of note reading if cases and sampled controls are read; interesting to the medical director and social work; novel for routine meetings in this hospital; ethical as secondary use of notes with a waiver request; relevant to a hospital-wide policy decision.
response.summary: One PECO question with the exposure defined as an attended meeting with a written plan.

response.rationale: The exposure worth studying is visible only in social work notes, which take about fifteen minutes each to read, and 120 hours are available. Reading notes for every eligible discharge since 2023 would take several times that, whereas sampling all readmitted cases (or a random sample of them) with two non-readmitted controls per case keeps reading within budget with little loss of precision (c3). Complexity drives both meetings and readmission (c2), so the design measures it from discharge summaries and adjusts for it. The retrieved evidence suggests the attended meeting with a written plan is the exposure to measure (c1).
alternatives: Cohort of all eligible discharges with note reading for everyone (refused: several hundred hours of reading)
Cohort using booked meetings from the activity log only (refused: measures the wrong exposure)
Randomised trial of standard family meetings (deferred: justified only if the local association is meaningful and the hospital is willing to randomise)
response.whyNotMoreComplex: A trial would answer the policy question directly but needs a signal and a willingness to withhold meetings; the case-control study uses existing notes to test whether the signal exists.

decision.statement: Answer the question with a case-control study: readmitted patients aged 75 and over and two frequency-matched non-readmitted controls per case, with an attended family meeting and written plan read from social work notes and case complexity measured from discharge summaries.
decision.question: Is an attended family discharge meeting with a written plan associated with fewer readmissions within 30 days in patients aged 75 and over?

store.title: Family discharge planning meetings and 30-day readmission in adults aged 75 and over

includes: Family discharge planning meetings and 30-day readmission in adults aged 75 and over

response.overview: Case-control study nested in discharges of patients aged 75 and over from the medical wards between January 2023 and December 2025, with exposure read from social work notes using a fixed abstraction form.
response.population: Eligible discharges: patients aged 75 and over discharged alive from the medical wards with a social work referral during the admission. Cases: 160 randomly sampled eligible discharges followed by an unplanned readmission within 30 days. Controls: 320 eligible discharges without readmission, frequency matched to cases by discharge quarter and ward group.
response.exposure: Primary: a family discharge planning meeting attended in person or by telephone by at least one family member or carer and ending with a written plan given to the family. Secondary: any booked meeting in the activity log. Unattended bookings form a separate category.
response.procedures: The informatics team draws cases from the readmission report and controls from the discharge list, and removes the readmission date from the reading packet. Two senior social workers read notes with the abstraction form, blind to case status where possible; 10 percent are read by both. Complexity (prior admissions in 12 months, frailty score, living alone, dementia, number of regular medicines, discharge destination) comes from the discharge summary.

outcomes.measure: Emergency readmission within 7 days, among cases
outcomes.why: Very early readmission is most plausibly linked to the discharge plan.

outcomes.why: Unreadable notes would bias the exposure.

outcomes.name: Reader agreement
outcomes.measure: Kappa for the primary exposure on the 10 percent read twice
outcomes.timing: After the first 100 notes and at the end
outcomes.why: Checks that the exposure is read consistently.

Readmission status hidden from readers where the notes allow

flags: Eight pre-specified covariates, two matching factors and six complexity measures
parsimony.simplestPath: One exposure contrast, one outcome, one adjusted logistic model.

response.theoreticalFramework: No framework beyond the case-control sampling design; the exposure definition follows the retrieved evidence on attended meetings.
response.summary: Case-control study of 160 cases and 320 frequency-matched controls with note-based exposure and complexity adjustment.

response.designSummary: Case-control study with frequency matching by discharge quarter and ward group; exposure is an attended meeting with a written plan.
response.sampleSize: With 160 cases and 320 controls and an exposure prevalence of about 25 percent among controls, the study has about 80 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 to detect an odds ratio of 0.50, and about 67 percent power for 0.55; smaller effects would be estimated imprecisely. 480 notes at fifteen minutes each use the 120 approved hours. The estimate will be reported with its confidence interval rather than as a significance verdict.
response.primaryAnalysis: Unconditional logistic regression of case status on the exposure, adjusted for the two matching factors and six complexity measures fixed in advance (prior admissions in 12 months, frailty score, living alone, dementia, number of regular medicines, discharge destination); about 16 cases per parameter.
response.secondaryAnalysis: The same model with the three-level exposure (attended with plan, booked but not attended, none); 7-day readmission among cases; an exploratory interaction with living alone reported without a significance claim.
response.missingData: Notes in which attendance cannot be determined are counted and reported; the primary analysis treats them as a separate category, with sensitivity analyses coding them first as exposed and then as unexposed; complexity measures missing for more than 5 percent are handled by multiple imputation.
response.multiplicity: One primary contrast; secondary and exploratory estimates are reported with confidence intervals and labelled as such.
response.software: R; the abstraction form, covariate list and analysis code archived before reading starts.
response.summary: 160 cases and 320 controls give about 80 percent power for an odds ratio of 0.50; adjusted logistic regression with complexity covariates fixed in advance.

response.risks: Minimal physical risk; the risk is privacy harm from reading identifiable social work notes, which contain sensitive family information.
response.consent: Consent is impracticable for 480 past discharges, some of whom have died; the research ethics board will be asked for a waiver of consent for secondary use under minimal risk, with notice on the hospital's research transparency page.
response.data: Readers work in the hospital's secure environment; the analysis file holds no names, hospital numbers or free text, only coded variables; the linkage key is held by the informatics team and destroyed after analysis.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: attendance depends on carers' work, transport and language, so families in deprived areas, working carers and families needing interpreters may be under-represented among attended meetings. Results will be reported by area deprivation quintile and by in-person versus telephone attendance, and any recommendation will address access to meetings, not only whether they are held.
response.effectiveness: The study informs whether standard meetings for everyone over 75 are worth social work time; a precise null result is as useful as a positive one.
response.efficiency: Uses existing notes and 120 approved hours; no patient contact.
response.costs: Social worker and informatics time within existing roles.
response.grants: None needed; a positive result would support an application for a trial of structured family meetings.
response.partnerships: Medical director's office (policy question), informatics team (sampling and linkage), two carer representatives from the hospital's carers' forum (exposure definition and interpretation), and the ward discharge coordinators.
response.rebPath: Full review by the hospital research ethics board for secondary use of identifiable social work notes with a waiver of consent, following ICH-GCP and Declaration of Helsinki principles; the board has not yet been asked, so the gate is unknown and no note is read before approval.
response.limitations: Residual confounding by family engagement; readmissions to other hospitals missed; notes may not record telephone attendance consistently.
response.summary: Secondary use of sensitive notes with a waiver request, equity reporting by deprivation and mode of attendance, and an ethics gate still unknown.

response.partnershipPlan: Two carer representatives from the carers' forum review the exposure definition and the plain-language summary; ward discharge coordinators advise on how meetings are recorded; the medical director's office receives interim reports only on progress, not results.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; anonymised compliments and complaints about discharge from the patient advice service in the last year are read for mentions of family meetings.

response.title: Attended family discharge planning meetings and 30-day readmission in adults aged 75 and over: a case-control study
response.abstract: Objective: to estimate the association between an attended family discharge meeting with a written plan and unplanned readmission within 30 days in adults aged 75 and over. Design: case-control study of 160 readmitted cases and 320 frequency-matched controls discharged from medical wards in 2023 to 2025, with exposure read from social work notes. Analysis: logistic regression adjusted for six measures of case complexity. Results and conclusions will be written after analysis.
response.introduction: Family involvement in discharge planning reduced readmission in trials, but routine meetings are chosen for complex patients, which makes crude comparisons misleading. The hospital is considering making meetings standard for patients over 75.
response.methods: Cases are unplanned readmissions within 30 days; controls are frequency matched by discharge quarter and ward group. Two senior social workers read notes with a fixed abstraction form, blind to case status where possible, with 10 percent read twice. Complexity is measured from discharge summaries. The analysis plan and covariates were fixed before reading.
response.results: No data have been analysed yet. The report will present sampling, reader agreement, the exposure distribution, crude and adjusted odds ratios, and the three-level exposure analysis.
response.discussion: The discussion will weigh the estimate against the retrieved trials and matched comparison, examine residual confounding by family engagement, and state what the result means for making meetings standard.
response.limitations: Residual confounding; readmissions elsewhere missed; exposure read from notes of variable quality.
response.conclusion: To be written after analysis; it will be limited to the association in this hospital and will not claim that meetings prevent readmission.
response.summary: STROBE-structured draft with results left empty until analysis.

path.problem.rawNeed:
I lead the hospital social work team at a 560-bed general hospital. For older patients with complicated discharges, our social workers sometimes hold a family discharge planning meeting on the ward before the patient goes home: the patient, family members or carers, the nurse in charge, often a therapist and the social worker go through the plan for care at home, equipment, help with medicines and who to call. Whether a meeting happens depends on which social worker has the case, whether the family can come in, and how rushed the discharge is.

Our medical director has asked whether these meetings reduce readmissions within 30 days, because the hospital pays a penalty for early readmissions of patients over 75 and is thinking of making family meetings standard for everyone over 75 with a complicated discharge. My worry is that we tend to hold meetings for the most complicated families, who are also the ones most likely to come back, so a simple comparison could make the meetings look useless or even harmful.

What we have: the hospital's monthly readmission report lists every patient readmitted within 30 days since January 2023, and our social work activity log shows when a family meeting was booked. The log does not say whether the family actually came, who attended or whether a written plan was given; that is only in the social work notes, and reading them takes about fifteen minutes per patient. Two of my senior social workers can give about 120 hours between them to reading notes this winter.

I do not know what kind of study this should be. Can you help me work out a fair way to answer the question with what we have, and what we would need to ask permission for?
